211.quote_or_event: “Man's duty is to give to those who are unable to bear (their distresses), not driving them away, nor turning away from the extended hands … to give to those who will pay it back again--has the name of a loan at interest.”
211.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār's chapter on liberality says true giving goes to the distressed who cannot repay, and that giving in expectation of a return is only lending at interest.
211.tie_back: Valluvar says duty to others expects nothing back, as the world repays nothing to the rain-cloud; the Nālaṭiyār makes the same point by calling a gift that expects repayment a loan at interest.
211.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 8 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
211._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (ellipsis marks an omitted vocative); this is a Tamil Jain text chosen as the closest fit, and it lacks the rain-cloud image (st. 7 of the same chapter pairs failing rain with failing duty).

212.quote_or_event: “Nyayasampannavibhavah : Possessed of honestly earned wealth.” … “Yathavat atithau sadhau dine cha pratipatti-krt : Diligent in succoring the ascetics, the righteous and the needy.”
212.explanation: Hemacandra's model Jain householder earns his wealth honestly and uses it to support ascetics, the righteous and the needy.
212.tie_back: Valluvar says wealth earned by hard effort exists to help the deserving; Hemacandra's ideal householder pairs honest earning with diligent support of worthy recipients.
212.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of thirty-five qualities of the ideal householder, items 1 and 19, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, Jaina Ethics (jainworld.com)
212._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com (Sangave's rendering, not a full Yogaśāstra translation); a strong fit, though the list sets the two qualities side by side and does not state that wealth exists for giving.

213.quote_or_event: “Those who are ten miles distant can hear the sound of the wide drum beaten with the stick; those a yojana distant, can hear the hoarse thunder; but all who live in the three worlds piled up will hear the report that some of the excellent have given alms.”
213.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār ends its chapter on liberality by saying the fame of generous giving reaches the whole three-tiered Jain universe, further than any drum or thunder.
213.tie_back: Valluvar says nothing in the world of the gods or on earth equals beneficence; the Nālaṭiyār likewise gives charity a renown that spans all three worlds.
213.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
213._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this is a Tamil Jain text. It is a partial fit: it praises the fame of giving across the worlds instead of saying giving is unequalled there.

214.quote_or_event: “The function of the souls (jīva) is to help one another.”
214.explanation: Umāsvāti's sūtra parasparopagraho jīvānām, now the motto of Jainism, defines what living beings do as mutual help; Pūjyapāda's commentary gives master and servant, teacher and pupil as examples.
214.tie_back: Valluvar says only the one who knows and does what is fitting toward the world is truly alive; Umāsvāti likewise defines the activity of living souls as helping one another.
214.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.21 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
214._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a strong thematic fit, though the sūtra is a metaphysical description of what souls do (it also covers causing each other pain), not a moral verdict that non-helpers are as good as dead.

215.quote_or_event: “He quitted and rejected his real, valuable property, such as riches, gold, precious stones, jewels, pearls, conches, stones, corals, rubies, &c.; he distributed presents through proper persons, he distributed presents among indigent persons.”
215.explanation: Before his renunciation Mahāvīra gave away his riches, distributing them through proper persons and to the poor.
215.tie_back: Valluvar compares a wise benefactor's wealth to a full village tank open to all; Mahāvīra's great giving before renunciation shows wealth turned into a common supply for the needy.
215.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §112 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
215._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (Jacobi); a reasonable fit, but this is a one-time gift made while renouncing the world, not the householder's lasting stewardship pictured by the tank.

216.quote_or_event: “Those who give are like the female palm tree surrounded by the terrace in the midst of the village, they live beloved by many. Men who eat without giving to others, though their family be flourishing, are like the male palm in a burning-ground.”
216.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār contrasts the generous person, like a fruit-bearing palm in the middle of the village, with the miser, like a barren palm in a cremation ground.
216.tie_back: Valluvar likens the generous man's wealth to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the village; the Nālaṭiyār uses almost the same image of a fruitful tree at the village centre.
216.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 6 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
216._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a near one-to-one parallel in image and point, from a Tamil Jain text closely related to the Kural, not from canonical scripture.

217.quote_or_event: “Charity (dāna) is the giving of one's objects to another for mutual benefit–anugraha.”
217.explanation: Umāsvāti defines charity as giving one's own wealth so that both sides benefit: the giver gains merit (puṇya) and the receiver is helped toward right knowledge and the like.
217.tie_back: Valluvar pictures a noble person's wealth as a healing tree that never fails others; the Jain definition of dāna also treats a good person's possessions as given out for others' benefit.
217.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.38 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
217._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a next-best match only. I found no verified Jain text with the medicinal-tree image, and this is a general definition of charity.

218.quote_or_event: The Master said compassionately: “Now I have abandoned all associations. Nevertheless, take half of this garment around my shoulder, sir.”
218.explanation: After giving away his wealth and becoming a monk, Mahāvīra is approached by Soma, a poor Brahman who missed the year of gifts, and gives him half of the only garment he has left.
218.tie_back: Valluvar says those who know their duty keep helping even when their means have shrunk; Mahāvīra, with nothing left but one cloth, still gives half of it.
218.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. III, part 1 'Loss of half of his garment' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
218._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a close narrative match from a 12th-century Śvetāmbara text, not the earliest canon.

219.quote_or_event: “Let a man who regards both this world and the next, give what he can as he gets it; and if, through poverty, giving be impossible, to abstain from begging will be to give twice.”
219.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār tells the generous to give whatever they can, and counts it as a double gift when someone too poor to give at least does not burden others by begging.
219.tie_back: Valluvar says that for the kind, poverty means only being unable to give; the Nālaṭiyār also treats poverty as the point where giving becomes impossible, and finds a form of giving even there.
219.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 10 ('Liberality'), st. 5 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
219._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this is a Tamil Jain text. It is a partial fit: it addresses giving and poverty, but not the anguish of being unable to give.

220.quote_or_event: The king said to him, “I will give you my own flesh, weighing it with the dove. Be satisfied. Do not die.” … When the king saw that the dove kept increasing in weight, he himself got on the scales with unequaled courage.
220.explanation: King Megharatha, in a former birth of the sixteenth Tīrthaṅkara Śāntinātha, protects a dove from a hawk by offering his own flesh and finally his whole body, while his ministers protest at the loss.
220.tie_back: Valluvar says that if helping others brings ruin, that ruin is worth buying even by selling oneself; Megharatha literally puts himself on the scales to save another being.
220.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book V (Śāntināthacaritra), ch. IV, part 7 'Story of the dove and hawk' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
220._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (ellipsis marks omitted narrative); a strong fit on giving oneself for another, though the Jain story frames it as protecting life (ahiṃsā), and the Buddhist Śibi tale is a known parallel.
